extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in First Amendment law, legal history, and censorship of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the legal criteria and evidentiary practices used to evaluate alleged obscene or indecent speech (especially live comedy performances and broadcasts), as illustrated by the Lenny Bruce Cafe Au Go Go trial and subsequent Supreme Court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penal Code 1140-A prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Penal Code 1140-A prohibited 'obscene, indecent, immoral, and impure dram, play, exhibition, and entertainment...which would tend to the corruption of the morals of youth and others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory language was the basis for the indictment against Bruce; prosecutions under this provision required showing the performance fell within that broad prohibition—i.e., that it tended to corrupt morals, particularly of youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show lustful/lecherous effect (prosecutorial burden argued by defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense contended that Supreme Court precedent required the prosecution to show that the defendant's words had inspired 'lustful and lecherous thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At issue in motions was whether coarse language alone sufficed or whether the prosecution needed to prove the words produced sexual arousal/impure thoughts in the audience; the court denied the defense motion to dismiss on these grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's three-part finding used in conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: The court concluded Bruce's act 'appealed to prurient interest,' was 'patently offensive to the average person in the community,' and lacked 'redeeming social importance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court applied these prongs to determine obscenity/indecency: prurient appeal, offensiveness to average person/community standards, and absence of redeeming social value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern obscenity definition (post‑1973 narrow standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court's current definition of obscenity (as of the 1973 case referenced) is very narrow: prosecutions would be allowed only for hard‑core pornography that is sexually explicit, patently offensive, and which lacks significant social, artistic, or political value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrows the scope of prosecutable material compared with earlier eras; the page contrasts this modern test with the broader standards applied in Bruce's time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between indecency and obscenity (and protection of emotive content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen (1971) recognized that the First Amendment protects not just intellectual content but emotive content as well; indecency (as distinct from obscenity) remains regulable in certain contexts like broadcasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cohen decision protected the choice of words as expressive (emotive) conduct, limiting obscenity prosecutions for mere vulgarity; however, indecency on public airwaves can be restricted for reasons like protecting children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting/ FCC channeling authority for indecency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court upheld the FCC's authority to channel broadcasts containing indecent words to late‑night hours, based on the public ownership of the airwaves, broadcasts' ability to reach listeners without warning, and the need to protect children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if speech is protected in other contexts, broadcasters may face time‑of‑day restrictions and fines for indecent material; the example is Carlin's 'Seven Dirty Words'—airing it could lead to FCC sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community standards / 'average person in the community' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The court evaluated whether material was 'patently offensive to the average person in the community' and defense experts testified about local community standards and everyday usage of 'dirty words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony about whether certain words are in daily use or offensive in the local community is used to inform the community‑standard prong; what the average community member finds offensive matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redeeming social importance / artistic or social value
rubrics_metrics.description: A key defense argument was that Bruce's language and routines had redeeming social importance as social satire and artistic expression—testimony by critics and scholars asserted artistic purpose and social commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether allegedly obscene material has social, artistic, political, or literary value; credible expert testimony that the material serves such functions can defeat obscenity/indecency findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary use of transcripts and tapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutors relied on a typed transcript (made from an often unintelligible tape) and audiotapes of performances to present evidence to a grand jury and at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality and clarity of recordings/transcripts affect prosecution; transcription errors or unintelligibility can create disputes over what was actually said. Tape evidence was central to the indictment process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and role of expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Both sides called experts—psychiatrists to testify about arousal, media experts about local standards, critics and academics about social value—to support or rebut claims about offensiveness and social importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony is used to establish (or refute) whether material is sexually arousing, offensive to local standards, or has literary/social merit; the composition and credibility of experts can sway judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert credibility and relevance (impeachment of experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert's credibility could be challenged by showing a lack of recent relevant experience (e.g., Van den Haag admitted he hadn't been to a nightclub in twenty years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess not just opinions but the qualifications and contemporaneity of experts; impeaching an expert's experience can diminish the weight of their testimony regarding community standards or social value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical gestures and nonverbal conduct as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution introduced testimony alleging that Bruce made masturbatory gestures with the microphone; such nonverbal conduct was used to support claims of obscenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscene conduct can be both verbal and physical; allegations about gestures or stage behavior can be treated as part of the overall assessment of whether a performance is obscene or appeals to prurient interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial discretion when standards are unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time of Bruce's prosecution the law relating to obscenity and indecency was 'in chaos' with no five‑member Supreme Court consensus, leaving much discretion to prosecutors, judges, and juries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When higher‑court standards are fractured, enforcement depends heavily on local officials' choices; this uncertainty forces performers to choose between calculated risks and self‑censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties, sentencing exposure, and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statute Bruce faced up to three years per charge; he was ultimately sentenced (in this account) to 'four months in the workhouse.' Post‑conviction remedies mentioned include appeals, appellate reversal, and gubernatorial pardon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal penalties can be severe and have long‑term personal/professional consequences; remedies include appellate review (possible reversal) and executive clemency or pardon (symbolic and practical relief).
